title: Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t.
author: Eli Hager
content:
It wasn’t the kind of call a grocery store gets every day. A customer with a
thick Eastern European accent was on the phone saying he wanted to buy several
thousand cans of Red Bull. Could the store have them in stock in a few days?
Also, did they have equipment to move all those stacks of energy drinks into
the parking lot, where two minivans would be waiting?

When the day came, Oct. 19, 2022, employees at the Smart & Final store in San
Diego sold 3,960 cans of Red Bull and 720 of Monster Energy to two men and two
women, all with the same accent, and helped them wheel the pallets out back.
To pay for it all — the bill came to $10,747.05 — the group pulled out piles
of plastic. These weren’t credit or debit cards; they looked more like hotel-
room keys. There were 25 cards in all, each with a different amount loaded
onto it, and the four people took turns swiping one after another. Then, the
payment complete, they drove off.

In the days that followed, people as far away as New York and Florida made
panicked calls to the store. They wanted to know why their food-stamp accounts
(containing their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP,
benefits) had been drained at this seemingly random location in San Diego.

It would turn out that what became known as the Red Bull Crew had gotten ahold
of their SNAP data and used the funds to buy the energy drinks, which they
then sold online or to smaller stores. It was hardly an isolated event. From
September through November of that year, the same crew, part of a criminal
syndicate based in Romania, bought at least $305,274.52 in energy drinks,
using SNAP account information and PINs stolen from at least 174 victims
nationwide, according to court documents and federal investigators.

To hear the Trump administration tell it, the SNAP program is under siege by
well-heeled recipients of food stamps. Vice President JD Vance, upon being
named [“Fraud Czar”](https://time.com/article/2026/04/03/trump-vance-fraud-
czar/) this spring, [said](https://x.com/VP/status/2051824964991410435):
“There are people who have Lamborghinis who currently receive SNAP benefits.”
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, whose agency oversees the program,
regularly goes on TV and social media to allege that masses of SNAP recipients
are scamming the system, driving [Bentleys, Ferraris,
Maseratis](https://x.com/SecRollins/status/2049131612835586505?s=20) and, yes,
Lamborghinis.

The federal government’s own statistics tell a different story. Confirmed
cases of intentional program violations — fraud — committed by SNAP recipients
account for $64 million a year, or about 0.08% of all benefits issued
annually, according to the most recent [50-state reports](https://fna-
bwbufwdzbabpezgc.z01.azurefd.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/snap-sar-
fy23.pdf) compiled by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Meanwhile a far bigger fraud wave has exploded over the past five years:
organized theft _from_ SNAP recipients. In 2025, $470 million was stolen
electronically from beneficiaries — and thus from the U.S. taxpayer —
according to data supplied to ProPublica by [Propel](https://www.propel.app/),
a company that provides a mobile app for SNAP recipients to check their
account balances and transaction histories. More than 990,000 households that
received food assistance last year had benefits stolen. (The reason it’s
necessary to use data from a private company: The federal government has
stopped tracking rates of this crime.)

ProPublica interviewed nearly 100 victims of SNAP theft, federal prosecutors,
Secret Service agents, USDA officials, caseworkers and other experts to
understand what’s behind this phenomenon and why more isn’t being done to stop
it. The victims are almost all working people with families, or retirees, who
have struggled to afford groceries in the current economy. Most didn’t learn
about the crime until they were in a checkout line, only to have their benefit
card declined.

![A white man with glasses makes coffee in his
kitchen.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/WEB_20260925-Harper-SNAP-Theft-45.jpg?w=752)Jared
Chesnut, a laid-off software developer in Hoover, Alabama, had $893 in SNAP
benefits stolen from him in December: “I ate rice and grits the rest of the
month.” Rita Harper for ProPublica

Upon reporting the disappearance of their food assistance, victims are
informed that nothing can be done under current federal law. “The only thing
they said was that [my benefits] cannot be refunded unless they were lost due
to a natural disaster,” said one SNAP theft victim in Ohio. “They told me
they’d add my name to the list,” said another in rural Oregon. “They advised
if I feel the place is sketchy, don’t run my card there,” a victim in
Philadelphia said. Still another, in Virginia, added, “They even charged me $2
for a replacement card.”

Perhaps the most vexing aspect of all: The federal government knows how to
prevent the vast majority of this crime in a single step. Congress just hasn’t
been willing to take it.

* * *

SNAP theft is an old scheme applied to a new target. For years, scammers would
surreptitiously install skimming devices on card readers at ATMs, gas pumps
and corner stores. These devices could read the data on people’s cards as they
swiped — while a pinhole camera or overlay keypad captured their PINs — all of
which could be picked up later or sent via Bluetooth to someone sitting in a
nearby cafe or parking lot. This pilfered data, in turn, was used to make
online purchases, or it was loaded onto cloned cards to withdraw cash.

Skimming became exponentially more difficult when credit and debit card
companies installed digital microchips in the 2010s and then introduced tap-
to-pay. But one kind of card did not get the new chips: Electronic Benefits
Transfer, or EBT, cards, which people use to access SNAP and other public
assistance. These still rely on the 1960s-era magnetic-stripe technology that
skimmers can easily read.

EBT cards are not a particularly high-value target compared with bank cards.
(The average monthly SNAP benefit is about $350 per household.) But [funding
boosts to SNAP](https://healthyeatingresearch.org/research/the-impact-of-
increasing-snap-benefits-on-stabilizing-the-economy-reducing-poverty-and-food-
insecurity-amid-covid-19-pandemic/) during the pandemic temporarily increased
benefit amounts, and profits could be considerable if you skimmed hundreds of
people’s card information every month. Skimming teams, often run by Romanian
gangs, pivoted. With cloned magnetic-stripe cards, they started buying up huge
quantities of SNAP-eligible products like energy drinks and baby formula that
are easy to store and resell.

“We’ve started many, many briefings saying that one of the biggest ways we’re
going to fight this is to just get chips in the cards,” said Michael Peck,
assistant special agent in charge of the Secret Service’s Criminal
Investigative Division. Among the Secret Service’s lesser-known functions is
investigating many financial crimes, and Peck leads its efforts against
benefit theft. He said he and his team have delivered this message on Capitol
Hill both at committee meetings and to individual members of Congress.

Yet congressional leadership has continually blocked legislation that would
fund chip EBT cards nationally, despite universal support for the measure
among Democrats and significant support among the Republican rank and file.
For instance, House Committee on Agriculture Chairman Glenn Thompson, a
Republican from Pennsylvania, said [at a hearing in
March](https://www.youtube.com/live/BCALjyDnUHM?t=18720s) that chip technology
is “very effective.” But he shut down a bipartisan proposal to upgrade EBT
cards with chips, citing unspecified budgetary constraints. (“Chairman
Thompson is supportive of finding a fiscally responsible path forward for
implementing policy that supports chip cards,” a committee aide said in a
statement on his behalf. She added that “there was an appetite” for this
reform among Republicans, but that Democrats weren’t willing to “find the
budgetary offsets” for it.)

The Congressional Budget Office has yet to formally score the proposal, but
multiple Hill staffers said they were told the total cost would be in the
range of $215 million, as compared to the [$600 million-
plus](https://www.propel.app/insights/2026-propel-survey-ebt-theft/) annual
loss on theft of SNAP and other benefits.

![A woman pushes a grocery cart while shopping with her
family.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/WEB_20261007-Tina-Russell-SNAP-
Theft-002.jpg?w=752)Adrianna Puckett, of Oak Hill, Florida, was on maternity
leave from a gas station job in July when she lost $516 to SNAP thieves. “It
was just the worst time that this could have happened,” she said. “I had to go
back to work full time with a newborn.” Tina Russell for ProPublica

The main thing Congress has done about SNAP theft is to abandon a previous
effort to help victims. The federal government had, since late 2022, been
replacing people’s stolen funds, just as banks are required to do if your
debit card is hacked. As a result, [753,929
households](https://www.fna.usda.gov/data-research/data-visualization/snap-
replacement-stolen-benefits-dashboard) were compensated.

In December 2024, a bipartisan spending agreement that included a provision to
extend these reimbursements through 2028 was on the brink of becoming law. But
Elon Musk, who had been named a leader of the new Department of Government
Efficiency, [attacked the legislation more than 100
times](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/12/18/elon-musk-false-claims-
cr-00195252) on X, pushing to “defund everything.” (Musk did not reply to a
request for comment.) Trump then [sank the
deal](https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2024-12-18/what-made-it-
and-what-didnt-make-it-into-the-bipartisan-funding-bill). Victims of SNAP
theft can no longer get any of their benefits replaced. And with the
government off the hook for losses, there is now less incentive to put money
into the solution.

In the 22 months since, the Trump administration has gone on to [strip funds
for](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/FY-2027-Chapter-34-FNS.pdf)
addressing EBT theft from the USDA’s annual budget requests to Congress, while
cutting at least 650 of the staff of the federal Food and Nutrition
Administration, the subagency that oversees SNAP. More than half of the
technical experts whom the agency had hired to help it develop EBT card
security guidance have been pushed out, according to the [Government
Accountability Office](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-25-107964.pdf).

“Many of us who were working on fraud, we’ve left the federal government
entirely,” said Kym Ayodeji, who had been a data scientist in the SNAP program
until she departed this spring. (FNA, the agency she worked for, is also
responsible for tracking fraud committed by retailers, which is far more
prevalent than that committed by beneficiaries.) Ayodeji said she and her
colleagues had been working on ways to identify retailers where unusually
large quantities of certain items had been purchased and addresses where
purchases made with many different EBT cards were being delivered. Some of
this work was indefinitely delayed by firings, early retirements, [agency
reorganizations](https://www.fna.usda.gov/about/reorganization) and
[government shutdowns](https://abcnews.com/Politics/snap-benefits-run-dry-
government-shutdown-continues-states/story?id=127059480), she said.

## [Do You Administer SNAP or Medicaid Benefits? Help ProPublica Report on
America’s Safety Net.](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/snap-medicaid-
share-experience-with-propublica)

We want to hear from the officials and workers who help people navigate SNAP
and Medicaid, because no one knows these programs better.

[Share Your
Experience](https://airtable.com/appV0ZWf06Gew4yWB/pagLr7CSAR8lvPhQz/form)

SNAP is federally funded and supervised. Congress and the USDA traditionally
mandate, and pay much of the costs for, major changes to the system,
especially involving technical coordination between states. States evaluate
applicants and administer the accounts of those who are approved.

That said, states are allowed to adopt chip cards on their own. California has
nearly completed the transition, and Alabama and Oklahoma began rolling out
new cards this year. A handful of others initiated the process in recent
months — before the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, starting Oct. 1, [cut 50% of
states’ administrative funding for SNAP](https://www.newsweek.com/snap-and-
medicaid-will-change-dramatically-in-october-what-to-know-12485810), which
Alabama and the others had tapped to transition to chip technology.

The rest — about 40 states — have likely missed their window, unless Congress
acts. They’re also waiting for [regulatory
guidance](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eAgendaViewRule?pubId=202404&RIN=0584-AE99)
on EBT card security and chip card implementation that the USDA has been
claiming for nearly four years it is planning to publish. (The USDA Office of
Inspector General [has found
that](https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/documents/reports/2026-01/27801-0001-12_FR_FOIA_508_signed.pdf)
the agency’s failure to issue this has allowed the theft of at least $555
million in SNAP benefits.)

State-level SNAP administrators have also been overwhelmed with the hundreds
of new requirements that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has saddled them with.
For one, the law mandates that states adopt intensive new work requirements
for older adults and others, resulting in voluminous additional monthly
paperwork. And federal funds will be slashed even further next year if states
don’t scramble to reduce their “payment error rate,” a figure that measures
unintentional over- and underpayments in SNAP benefits. With all of this to
juggle, many state officials told ProPublica that they’ve [put chip card
implementation on hold](https://aphsa.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/2026-06_APHSA-State-SNAP-Survey-Results.pdf) in order
to implement the Trump law — one of whose ostensible goals was [to reduce
fraud](https://mikejohnson.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=2622).

All the while, that law has cut food aid for [more than 1.2 million
children](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/more-than-1-2-million-children-
have-lost-snap-benefits-since-last-july-experts-explain-why). The USDA’s
Rollins has said that nearly 6 million people in total [have been “moved off
SNAP”](https://bsky.app/profile/atrupar.com/post/3mvzy625hyk22) during the
current administration.

![A white woman in her 70s makes a meal in her
apartment.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/WEB_Kholood-
Eid_Ana-Marton_DSC6703.jpg?w=752)Ana Marton, a 75-year-old retired architect
in New York City, had $304 swiped from her SNAP account. “I am very vulnerable
at my age,” she said. “The insecurity that this could happen again is
immense.” Kholood Eid for ProPublica

The White House declined to respond to a detailed list of questions. A USDA
spokesperson, in an emailed statement, did not refute that Rollins has focused
on individual SNAP recipient fraud rather than on EBT theft, but said that
finding “cracks in public statements screams politics, not fact-finding.” The
spokesperson also did not address ProPublica’s reporting showing that the
agency has failed to deliver solutions on EBT theft specifically. Instead, the
statement pointed to the agency’s work, in collaboration with the Department
of Justice, combating retailer fraud. The USDA says it has cracked down on
thousands of stores that were abusing their SNAP privileges.

* * *

Absent action from Congress or USDA leadership, it has largely been left to
the Secret Service to apply an enforcement approach to what is arguably a
policy problem. Agents first went after gangs like the Red Bull Crew, often by
watching hours upon hours of grocery store surveillance footage. More
recently, they’ve tried to get ahead of the scammers by heading to cities that
have been hit by EBT theft attacks and then going store to store to check card
readers for skimming devices. The agency has run more than 70 of these
operations since April 2024, independent of any White House initiative.

![A person wearing blue gloves removes an overlay from a card reading machine
at a convenience store checkout counter.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/WEB_Zaydee-Sanchez-EBT-SS_139.jpg?w=1149)During an
operation in August in Burbank, California, a Secret Service analyst removes a
skimming device from a convenience store’s card reader. Zaydee
Sanchez/ProPublica

Most of them are led by Peck, the assistant special agent in charge. With his
form-fitting black polo tucked into cargo pants and a contoured beard, he has
a flat affect even as he lists off colorful details like how the criminals
sometimes ship dishwashers full of cash overseas. But he also emphasizes the
vulnerability of the victims and wishes there was even more his team could do
for them. “The U.S. has been fighting the War on Drugs and the War on Terror
for how many years?” he said. “We are pushing hard and we’re doing all we can
with the resources and abilities that we have.”

One bright morning in late June, dozens of law enforcement officers gathered
in a Secret Service meeting room on the top floor of a downtown Brooklyn
skyscraper, with a commanding view of the New York City skyline. In addition
to unarmed Secret Service analysts in short-sleeved shirts inscribed with the
field office they were joining from (Nashville, Miami, San Diego), there were
agents from the USDA Office of Inspector General as well as a smattering of
NYPD officers — who had guns, handcuffs and the jurisdiction to make arrests
should anything go awry that day.

From a podium, Peck recapped how the multiday New York operation was going so
far, including that the previous day, officers had happened upon two foreign
nationals installing a skimming device, chased them down and made arrests. “Be
safe, watch backs, stay fed,” he concluded.

Then everyone dispersed into teams of three or four. Each was given a list of
dozens of stores in Brooklyn or Queens — disproportionately ethnic and dollar
stores, but also some larger chains like 7-11 — that they were assigned to
visit, based on data analytics showing where skimming activity was most
probable.

The squad that ProPublica joined was headed to Midwood, in South Brooklyn,
which is home to Orthodox Jews and immigrants from the Middle East, Central
Asia and elsewhere. As we walked around the neighborhood with these federal
agents, we got plenty of confused looks and some scared ones, too.

“Hello, we’re here with the Secret Service,” one of the analysts would say
upon entering each store. Then they’d ask the store manager for permission to
inspect each card reader. They also handed out flyers in four languages
telling the cashiers what to look out for.

When they did find a skimming device, they donned gloves and masks to handle
it. After prying it off the card reader, they bagged it and tagged it, to be
sent in for DNA and fingerprint testing as well as digital forensic analysis.
Maybe a lead could be extracted, a connection to a larger EBT theft ring.

These missions are clearly well-intentioned, and every skimmer removed saves
families from being deprived of food. Yet, plainly, conducting store-to-store
checks of card readers is inefficient. Over the course of two years, the
agency has spent tens of thousands of staff hours checking 69,805 point-of-
sale terminals at stores, 42,972 gas pumps and 10,661 ATMs. They’ve found 637
skimming devices. And as one agent told ProPublica, “There could be a new
skimmer on there tomorrow.”

* * *

Ultimately, it just won’t be possible to arrest one’s way out of this crisis,
both federal and state law enforcement officials acknowledged. Low-level
runners keep arriving from Romania and elsewhere; even if they do get caught,
they’re often able to bond out of jail because they’re only facing state
charges for nonviolent offenses. Then they disappear.

Funding for chip EBT cards still faces dim prospects on Capitol Hill,
according to Democratic and Republican lawmakers and staffers, even with
[newfound](https://www.nationalgrocers.org/semtac/)
[support](https://www.convenience.org/advocate-for-the-
industry/issues/snap/snap-modernization-ebt-chip-cards) from major retailer
associations and big players like Walmart. There’s a chip card provision in
the Senate’s draft version of this year’s [Farm
Bill](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS22131), but the whole package is
mired in a dispute between the parties — over the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s
cuts to SNAP funding — that looks like it will last until well after the
midterm elections. This almost doesn’t matter, given that on the House side,
the Farm Bill has already passed, and it contains no funding for chip cards.

And there’s been no movement on [repeated bipartisan
proposals](https://meng.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/meng-lawler-
fetterman-introduce-bipartisan-bill-return-stolen-snap) from Sen. John
Fetterman of Pennsylvania and others to renew the reimbursement program for
families that have had their food assistance taken.

![A Black woman wearing denim overalls poses for a portrait in front of the
Pittsburgh skyline.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/WEB_Zaydee-Sanchez-EBT-Pam-Harris.jpg?w=752)Pamela
Harris, a retired IT worker in Pittsburgh, had $298 stolen: “I had to dig into
my Social Security and put my utility bills on hold to buy food.” Zaydee
Sanchez/ProPublica

Certainly, the mass distribution of any new payment technology isn’t easy.
California, Alabama and Oklahoma have had to phase in their new cards
gradually, allowing customers to still use the card’s magnetic stripe if the
chip isn’t working everywhere yet. And they’ve tried to notify rural
convenience stores and gas stations, and help corner bodegas update their card
readers, so that no one is left with only a chip card in a desert of stores
that still just accept magnetic stripe.

But by doing all of this and employing additional data tools, California has
reduced the theft of food and cash benefits [by as much as
83%](https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/01/16/california-reduces-theft-of-food-and-
cash-benefits-by-83-with-state-of-the-art-technology/) in just two years, the
governor’s office said. And Alabama officials claim their state hasn’t had any
confirmed EBT theft cases since they began to distribute chip cards this year.

Still, chip cards aren’t the entire solution and doubtlessly, scammers will
find clever ways to get around this technology. Moreover, SNAP recipients have
largely been denied the basic services that banks and credit card companies
use to block likely fraudulent transactions in real time. (Think of the email
or text alerts you get from your bank when suspicious purchases are attempted
with your card information.)

If [states were to try this](https://www.aspeninstitute.org/news/aspen-
institute-financial-security-program-launches-pilot-program-to-protect-
families-from-ebt-theft/) without federal help, they would have to
individually pay for the additional security features. Most have gone for
cheaper options like advising or requiring SNAP recipients to change their PIN
regularly and to lock their card when not using it. Both are useful stopgaps
but require constant diligence.

State and county SNAP caseworkers said they’ve been deeply frustrated that
ever since Trump and Musk killed the reimbursement program, all they can do
for victims is suggest they change their PIN more often and maybe try
reporting the crime to local law enforcement. “It is a short conversation,”
said Norman Vogele, a caseworker in Oregon. The date of the crime and the
missing amount is recorded. “It isn’t clear why we even do that much,” he
said, “as there is zero recourse.”

* * *

The Red Bull Crew stayed on the run for over a year, using looted food
benefits to buy hundreds of thousands of dollars of bulk energy drinks in
Oklahoma, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. After hundreds
of hours of surveillance by the Secret Service, federal prosecutors and local
authorities, all but one of the members were arrested and served sentences
ranging from one to three years. They’ve all since been released, and some may
have been deported.

Meanwhile, every day, SNAP theft sprees keep popping up in new corners of the
country. A Secret Service official sounded gloomy about the pursuit of street-
level operatives on its own, without policy change. “You can arrest them,” he
said. “But essentially once you take them off the street, there’s 10 more that
are doing the same thing.”
